title: Arduino: The Simpler Cousin
description: Component lesson. A second common board, and honestly: why two boards exist, and when to pick which.

content.value: If the ESP32 does so much, why does anyone still use anything else? Because "does more" isn't always what a project needs. Arduino boards — the Uno is the classic one — strip things back to just a processor and pins, no wireless radio, and that simplicity is exactly the point for a lot of beginner projects.

ESP32              Arduino Uno
Wi-Fi/Bluetooth     yes                 no
GPIO pins           ~34                 ~20
Logic voltage       3.3V                5V
Clock speed         240 MHz             16 MHz
Beginner-friendly   yes                 yes, and slightly simpler
Price               ≈ ₹450              ≈ ₹550

Notice the voltage row: Arduino Uno's pins are 5V logic, which happens to match a lot of older sensor modules built before 3.3V boards were common. That's often the real deciding factor, more than raw power.

They're not really competitors — they're tools for different jobs. If a project needs Wi-Fi, more pins, or more processing power, the ESP32 wins easily. If a project is small, doesn't need wireless, and needs to wire up cleanly to 5V parts, Arduino's simplicity and huge library of ready-made example code can make it the faster build.

ARIA uses an ESP32 because this course eventually wants Wi-Fi (Module 11's remote control and voice features need it), but almost everything you learn about pins, digital signals and PWM in this module works identically on either board — the concepts don't belong to one chip.

"Arduino" is also the name of the beginner-friendly programming environment both boards can be coded in, which is part of why the two names get used together so often — the board and the toolchain share a name.
Key takeaway: Arduino boards trade away wireless for simplicity and 5V compatibility. Neither board is strictly better — the right one depends on what the project needs.

quiz.question: What does a classic Arduino Uno leave out that the ESP32 includes?
quiz.explain: Arduino Uno has no wireless radio at all — that stripped-down simplicity is its main trade-off against the ESP32.

quiz.question: A project needs to wire up several older 5V sensor modules and never needs Wi-Fi. Which board fits more naturally?
options: Arduino Uno, since its 5V logic matches the sensors directly
Neither board can wire up a 5V sensor
quiz.explain: Matching logic voltage avoids needing a level-shifter. When wireless isn't needed, Arduino's 5V pins can be the simpler match.

quiz.question: Why does ARIA use an ESP32 rather than an Arduino Uno?
options: Because Arduino boards can't run any code
Because later modules need Wi-Fi for remote control and voice features
quiz.explain: The deciding factor is future needs — Module 11's autonomous and remote-control features rely on the wireless the ESP32 already has built in.
